title: Linux on Raspberry Pi
subtitle: systemd services, cron jobs, logging, and running code at boot
author: Kernal Team

whyItExists.problem: A Raspberry Pi that only works when you're logged in and manually running a script isn't useful as a deployed device. Real embedded Pi projects must run reliably at boot, restart after crashes, and log their output for diagnosis.
whyItExists.solution: systemd is the init system on Raspberry Pi OS. Creating a .service unit file lets your Python script start automatically at boot, restart on failure, and integrate with journalctl for log viewing. cron handles scheduled tasks.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any Pi project meant to run unattended: sensor loggers, home servers, media players, kiosk displays, IoT hubs.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Development phase — start with direct script execution. Only wrap in systemd when the project is stable enough to deploy.

explainModes.beginner: When you deploy a Raspberry Pi somewhere, you need your Python script to start automatically when the Pi powers on and restart itself if it crashes. systemd is the tool that does this — it's like a supervisor for your programs.
explainModes.simple: Create a .service file describing your script, copy it to /etc/systemd/system/, then run systemctl enable to start it at boot and systemctl start to run it now. Use journalctl -u yourservice to see the logs.
explainModes.standard: systemd unit files define a service's start command, working directory, restart policy, and dependencies (like network.target for internet-dependent scripts). Services run as a specific user and log to the journal automatically without any extra log setup.
explainModes.technical: systemd uses cgroup-based resource tracking. Service types: simple (default, main process), forking (daemonises), notify (signals readiness), oneshot (runs and exits). The WantedBy directive creates symlinks in multi-user.target.wants/. TimeoutStopSec and KillSignal control shutdown behavior.
explainModes.deepDive: systemd socket activation allows a service to start only when a connection arrives on a socket. For resilient Pi projects: use `Restart=always`, `RestartSec=5`, `StartLimitIntervalSec=0` (no restart limit). Add `MemoryMax=` to prevent a runaway script from consuming all SRAM. Watchdog integration: set `WatchdogSec=30` and have the service call `sd_notify(WATCHDOG=1)` or use `systemd-notify`.

content.text: Running Scripts at Boot with systemd

systemd is the init system on Raspberry Pi OS. It starts and supervises all system processes. To run your Python script as a service, create a .service unit file and register it with systemd. This gives you automatic startup, crash recovery, and centralised logging.

content.code:
[Unit]
Description=Sensor Data Logger
Documentation=https://github.com/yourname/sensor-logger
After=network.target  # start after network is up
Wants=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=pi
Group=pi
WorkingDirectory=/home/pi/sensor-logger
Environment=PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
ExecStart=/home/pi/sensor-logger/venv/bin/python main.py

# Auto-restart on crash
Restart=always
RestartSec=5
StartLimitIntervalSec=0  # no limit on restart attempts

# Log to journal
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal
SyslogIdentifier=sensor-logger

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

# 1. Copy service file
sudo cp sensor-logger.service /etc/systemd/system/

# 2. Reload systemd to pick up new file
sudo systemctl daemon-reload

# 3. Enable: start at every boot
sudo systemctl enable sensor-logger.service

# 4. Start now (without rebooting)
sudo systemctl start sensor-logger.service

# 5. Check status
sudo systemctl status sensor-logger.service

# 6. View live logs (Ctrl+C to stop)
journalctl -u sensor-logger.service -f

# 7. View last 50 lines
journalctl -u sensor-logger.service -n 50 --no-pager

# Common control commands:
# sudo systemctl stop    sensor-logger   # stop
# sudo systemctl restart sensor-logger   # restart
# sudo systemctl disable sensor-logger   # don't start at boot

content.text: Always use a Python virtual environment in your service: `ExecStart=/home/pi/myproject/venv/bin/python main.py`. This isolates dependencies and avoids conflicts between projects. Create the venv with `python3 -m venv venv` inside the project directory.
cron runs commands on a time schedule. Use crontab -e to edit your user's cron table. Common patterns: hourly data upload, daily log rotation, weekly backups.

content.code:
# Edit your user's cron jobs
crontab -e

# Crontab format:
# min  hour  day  month  weekday  command
#  *    *     *     *       *

# Example cron jobs:
# Run sensor upload every 5 minutes
*/5 * * * * /home/pi/scripts/upload_sensor.py >> /home/pi/logs/upload.log 2>&1

# Run backup every day at 2:30 AM
30 2 * * * /home/pi/scripts/backup.sh >> /home/pi/logs/backup.log 2>&1

# Reboot Pi every Monday at 4 AM (keep Pi fresh)
0 4 * * 1 /sbin/reboot

# Run on reboot
@reboot sleep 30 && /home/pi/scripts/startup.py >> /home/pi/logs/startup.log 2>&1

# View current cron jobs
crontab -l

content.text: All systemd services log to the journal automatically. journalctl is your primary debugging tool for deployed Pi projects. The journal survives service crashes and stores structured logs with timestamps.

content.code:
# Live stream logs from your service
journalctl -u sensor-logger -f

# Last 100 lines
journalctl -u sensor-logger -n 100 --no-pager

# Logs since yesterday
journalctl -u sensor-logger --since yesterday

# Logs between specific times
journalctl -u sensor-logger --since "2026-11-14 09:00" --until "2026-11-14 10:00"

# Only errors
journalctl -u sensor-logger -p err

# System boot logs
journalctl -b   # current boot
journalctl -b -1 # previous boot (useful after crash)

# Disk usage of journal
journalctl --disk-usage

# Limit journal size (edit /etc/systemd/journald.conf)
# SystemMaxUse=50M

content.text: File Permissions and Python Script Best Practices

content.code:
# Make Python script executable
chmod +x /home/pi/myproject/main.py
# Add shebang line at top of main.py:
# #!/home/pi/myproject/venv/bin/python

# Fix file ownership
chown -R pi:pi /home/pi/myproject/

# Create log directory with correct permissions
mkdir -p /home/pi/logs
chown pi:pi /home/pi/logs

# Test run as the pi user (before systemd)
sudo -u pi /home/pi/myproject/venv/bin/python /home/pi/myproject/main.py

# Check what a running service is doing
sudo lsof -p $(systemctl show -p MainPID sensor-logger | cut -d= -f2)

content.title: systemd Service vs cron for Automation

a.name: systemd Service
a.useWhen: Long-running servers, sensor pollers, MQTT clients — anything that runs indefinitely

b.name: cron Job
b.useWhen: Periodic uploads, cleanup scripts, backups — tasks that run and exit

content.text: When a systemd service needs to access GPIO, it must run as the `pi` user (or add the user to the `gpio` group) — running as root is unnecessary and a security risk. Add `User=pi` and `Group=pi` to your .service file, and ensure the user is in the `gpio` and `i2c` groups: `sudo usermod -aG gpio,i2c,spi pi`.

questions.question: What systemd command makes a service start automatically at every boot?
questions.explanation: `systemctl enable` creates the symlink in /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/ that causes the service to start at boot. `systemctl start` only starts it once for the current session.

questions.question: How do you view live log output from a systemd service called 'sensor-logger'?
questions.explanation: `journalctl -u sensor-logger -f` streams live logs from the sensor-logger service. The -u flag filters by unit name; -f follows the stream like tail -f.

questions.question: What does the cron entry `*/5 * * * * /home/pi/upload.py` do?
options: Runs upload.py once at minute 5 of every hour
Runs upload.py every 5 minutes, every hour, every day
Runs upload.py on the 5th day of every month
questions.explanation: */5 in the minutes field means 'every 5 minutes'. The remaining * fields (hour, day, month, weekday) mean 'any', so the command runs every 5 minutes around the clock.

faq.q: How do I schedule a script to run every 5 minutes?
faq.a: Edit crontab with `crontab -e` and add: `*/5 * * * * /home/pi/venv/bin/python /home/pi/script.py >> /home/pi/logs/script.log 2>&1`. The 2>&1 redirects stderr to the same log file so you capture errors.

faq.q: My service starts but then stops immediately. How do I diagnose it?
faq.a: Run `journalctl -u yourservice -n 50 --no-pager` to see the last 50 log lines including any Python tracebacks. Also run the ExecStart command manually from the terminal as the same user (e.g., `sudo -u pi /path/to/venv/bin/python main.py`) to see errors directly.

faq.q: Can a systemd service start before WiFi is connected?
faq.a: Yes, unless you tell it not to. Add `After=network-online.target` and `Wants=network-online.target` (instead of just network.target) to wait until the network interface has an IP address before starting. Also enable the network-online service: `sudo systemctl enable systemd-networkd-wait-online`.
